title: Which Warnings to Believe: The Compiler's Opinions, Counted and Judged

questions.question: A build reports 98 warnings, all the same message from the same header. What is the most likely number of defects?
options: Ninety eight, since each line is a separate place in the code
It cannot be estimated without reading all 98
Somewhere near 98, minus duplicates from the same line
One, because a warning is reported per translation unit and a header is compiled once per file that includes it
questions.explanation: Measured: one bad comparison in one header, three source files including it, gave 3 warning lines at 1 distinct site. This repository's own 98 of -Wclobbered came from a single setjmp structure.

questions.question: The same source file gave gcc 4 warning lines and clang 3. Why?
options: gcc counts notes as warnings and clang does not
The file had a compiler-specific #ifdef in it
gcc reports a partially braced struct once per missing member, clang once per brace
clang stops after three warnings by default
questions.explanation: Both reported 3 distinct sites. So a count is not even comparable between compilers, which is another reason to count sites rather than lines.

questions.question: 51 warnings of -Wmismatched-new-delete were investigated and found to be false. Why did a #pragma GCC diagnostic fail to suppress them?
options: It is emitted in a late pass after inlining, where the lexical region the pragma describes no longer exists
It did suppress them, but only in debug builds
The pragma was in the wrong file
Pragmas cannot suppress warnings that mention operator delete
questions.explanation: The pragma was tried and reverted, because leaving it would have implied a suppression that was not happening. gcc was failing to model that both global operators had been replaced; the address sanitizer independently confirmed the pairing was correct.

questions.question: Pose p = {1.5}; warns as -Wmissing-field-initializers. What is the warning actually asking for?
options: Nothing; the line is undefined behaviour and must be rewritten
Default member initialisers in the type, which silence the identical brace on both compilers
A cast, because 1.5 is a double and the members may not be
The remaining members written out explicitly at every call site
questions.explanation: The line is completely defined: unmentioned members are value initialised. The warning means the compiler cannot tell whether you meant it, so the answer belongs in the type, permanently, rather than at the call site.

questions.question: -Wdelete-non-virtual-dtor is silent for which case, and why does that matter?
options: It is never silent; it warns on every non-virtual destructor
A base with a protected destructor, which is already safe
An abstract base, since it cannot be instantiated
A base with no virtual functions at all, which is the shape a handle or resource wrapper has and exactly the case that bites
questions.explanation: Nothing marks such a class as polymorphic, so the compiler has no reason to suspect it is a base. Measured silent on both gcc and clang, which is why lesson 03-10's answer is a static_assert rather than a warning.

questions.question: Why does this curriculum compile checks/ with -Werror but not the lesson targets?
options: -Werror is unavailable on one of the four toolchains
checks/ files are the only ones that produce warnings
A learner's first warning should be a message they can read and decide about
The lesson targets would not compile with -Werror
questions.explanation: A course that fails the build on a warning in lesson four teaches them to switch warnings off. A checks/ snippet is not the learner's code, it is an assertion about what a compiler will refuse, so it is compiled the way a project that means it would. A real project should turn -Werror on, and what makes that bearable is counting sites and keeping a written ledger of the warnings already dismissed.
